description: Cluster 1 is the third largest cluster, and it discusses the implications of socially responsible investment (SRI) and corporate social responsibility (CSR) on companies’ financing costs. CSR and sustainable development are controversial topics among scholars (Kolsi and Attayah 2018) with two opposing views. According to the first view, corporations are not capable of carrying social responsibility costs. Thus, companies engaging in CSR will suffer from a reduction in their economic and financial positions, which will have a negative impact on their capacity to ensure sustainable operations and development. In contrast, the second view sees that corporations are responsible for protecting the plant and the environment, and they should have a balance between CSR’s associated cost and their social responsibility. The importance of CSR cannot be ignored due to many factors. First, customers are paying more attention to the topic of corporate social responsibility, and companies’ view of CSR may affect their market shares and customers’ loyalty. Second, employees are now more aware and willing to participate in protecting the environment and in adding value to their direct communities (Moon 2007; Alrayyes and Al Khaldy, 2019; Derbali, 2021). Therefore, JSFI is paying attention to the field of corporate social responsibility and sustainable development. After the last financial crisis, scholars have paid more attention to the financial sector’s role in CSR and in contributing to sustainable development (Weber 2014). In this cluster, articles discuss many aspects, including the environmental aspects and credit risk management (Weber, Hoque, and Ayub Islam 2015), the implication of CSR on stock return (Chen, Hung, and Lee 2017; Jamile and Diab, 2021), controlling investors and CSR (Rees and Rodionova 2013; Ahmad and Abu-Ghunmi, 2021), and the impact of capital structure on CSR. Cluster 2 is the second-largest cluster and focuses on a topic that has increasingly been attracting the attention of both scholars and professionals, which is the relationship between finance and environmental sustainability. Investment decisions should consider financial returns, as well as environmental and social benefits. Moreover, this cluster discusses green bonds, whose market has seen exponential growth since its start in 2007. In 2019, the annual issuance of green bonds was USD 228.2 billion, as compared to USD 40.6 billion in 2015. This significant increase (a growth of 462%) shows the investors’ growing demand for financial investments that serve a positive social purpose (Mankata et al. 2020). The growth in the green bond markets ensures the importance of sustainable investment and the significance of integrating economic, social, governance and environmental outcomes into fixed income portfolios. This theme should be reinforced by discussing new related topics such as Sukuks. In this cluster, important aspects are investigated tackling sustainable finance and green bonds, such as sustainable investment and firm performance (Boulatoff and Boyer 2017; Al-Afifi, 2019), corporate governance and sustainable finance (Shrivastava and Addas 2014; Alazemi and Al Omari, 2020), and financial sector openness and renewable energy investments (Koengkan, Fuinhas, and Vieira 2020). Although several review studies on this relation are published, the largest one analyses just a fraction of the studies. Thus, to overcome this limitation of not having a deep review of studies on this relation, Friede, Busch, and Bassen (2015) extract and combine the findings of 2200 studies. They find that only 10% of studies reported a negative impact of ESG on financial performance, while the majority of studies documented a positive impact of ESG on the firm’s financial performance. This cluster attracts the second-highest citations per document, with 5.65 citations per document. The reason for this high average citation is the paper of Friede, Busch, and Bassen (2015) that harvested 212 citations. Excluding this paper will reduce the average to 3.98 citations per document. The last cluster, being the smallest cluster, examines responsible investment and pension funds. For example, one article examines whether pension funds’ fiduciary duty should be extended to include social, ethical, and environmental concerns. There is a debate among fund managers, lawyers, and academics concerning the extent to which pension funds should be socially responsible in their investment decisions. On one side, the legal responsibility of pension funds, also known as the fiduciary duty, is to manage their funds in the best interests of the recipients of the funds, known as beneficiaries. Best interests are defined as short-term financial interests. However, this view has been challenged, and a common argument is that best interests should be interpreted more broadly to also include other concerns such as beneficiaries’ ethical or welfare interests. This controversy is resolved by measuring preferences for socially responsible investment (SRI) among pension funds’ beneficiaries (Jansson et al. 2014; Khalaf and Al-Tarawneh, 2019; Awad et al., 2021 Hasan and Hassan, 2021) Another topic is the influence strategies used by pension funds in shareholder engagement. Since pension funds are becoming significant owners of corporations and given their long-term investment horizon, they consider environmental, social and governance risks in their investment decision. More specifically, since ESG violations do not only damage the reputation of the portfolio firm, but also its shareholders, owners like pension funds have a strong incentive to improve environmental and social standards at the firm level to reduce the risk of damage to their reputations. Thus, the choice of influence strategies by pension funds to promote shareholder engagement is important to mitigate risk and maintain reputation. More specially, successful shareholder engagements can lead to more sustainable corporate behaviour and a lower risk to the investor. Thus, Hamilton and Eriksson (2011) try to identify a set of influence strategies used in shareholder engagement, which are closely intertwined with the fund’s risk reputation and management (Hamilton and Eriksson 2011; Al Kurdi, 2021; Alnoaimi and Mazzuchi, 2021).
